phases: If It Were Up to Me

listenings.text: The thing nobody tells you about a business dinner is that the first twenty minutes decide the whole evening, and almost nobody prepares for them. People prepare the pitch. Nobody prepares the small talk. I have sat at tables where somebody brought up the contract before the starters arrived, and you could feel the temperature drop. What I do now, and I would recommend this to anyone, is I find one thing before I get there. One thing. Where they went to university, a city we have both lived in, a team they support. If I were starting again, that is the only skill I would work on, because everything else you can prepare on a plane. And read the room. If the table goes quiet after somebody mentions work, that is information. Do not fill the silence with more work.

I would not say one is better than the other, but they are not the same evening. With some of the partners I work with, dinner is the meeting. Nothing is signed at the table, nothing is even discussed at the table, and then two days later everything moves, and it moves because of the dinner. With others, dinner is genuinely dinner. It is forty minutes, it is friendly, and then somebody says right, shall we talk about the numbers. The mistake I made for years was assuming, and if I could give myself one piece of advice it would be this: ask. Ask the person who invited you what the evening is for. Nobody has ever been offended by that question, and I have been wrong about it more often than I have been right.
